one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) opinion obtained by international celebrity lawyer Amal Alamuddin Clooney, holding that 'the detention of former President [Gloria Macapagal] Arroyo (GMA) was arbitrary and illegal under international law ... with an enforceable right to compensation.' Communications Secretary Coloma responded that GMA 'has been accorded due process and has availed herself of various legal remedies ... in Philippine courts, which have sole jurisdiction to decide on such matters.' CJ adds that the controversy is about a mere opinion of a UN working group lacking the coercive power of a treaty, customary international law, or a decision after trial of an international tribunal like the ICJ, ICC, or Itlos (where the PH WPS claim is being heard). GMA faces two major suits: electoral sabotage (a capital offense) in RTC Pasay for alleged manipulation of the 2007 Maguindanao election results, and plunder (also a capital offense) in the SBN for alleged participation in the illegal use of P366 million in PCSO funds. RTC granted bail on sabotage (affirmed by CA) because the prosecution failed to prove evidence of guilt is strong, but SBN denied bail on plunder. After the prosecution rested in the PCSO case, the defense filed a demurrer arguing the evidence failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the Special SBN Division voted 3-2 denying the demurrer and ruling the prosecution had proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt -- unless GMA presents countervailing evidence, she would be at risk of conviction. Significantly -- noted in the WGAD opinion -- the demurrer of her four coaccused (former PCSO chair Manuel Morato, former PCSO board members Raymundo Roquero and Jose Taruc, former COA chair Reynaldo Villar) was granted, resulting in their acquittal; former PCSO chair Sergio Valencia was downgraded to malversation (not a capital offense) with P500,000 bail; only GMA and former PCSO executive Benigno Aguas remain neither acquitted nor bailed. Failing in demurrer and bail, GMA filed a motion to transfer confinement from Veterans Memorial Medical Center to her home at 14 Badjao Street, La Vista, Quezon City; in view of the WGAD opinion, she is renewing her plea for bail. CJ believes more compelling than the WGAD opinion -- which, as Coloma pointed out, is not binding on our judiciary -- is the recent SC decision Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan (Aug 18, 2015) granting bail to Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile not because the Ombudsman failed to present 'strong' evidence of guilt but because of (1) Enrile's 'fragile' health (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary calcifications, exacerbations of asthma-COPD overlap syndrome) and (2) advanced age (over 70 at the time of the alleged offense). Veering from 'strong evidence of guilt' as the sole constitutionally-mandated bail ground in capital offenses, the Court said the SBN 'arbitrarily ignored the objective of bail to ensure the appearance of the accused during the trial.' True, the 8-4 decision was heavily criticized by Justice Marvic Leonen's dissent -- but whether we agree or not, once affirmed final (through denial of the pending MR), it becomes binding precedent. Citing equal protection, GMA's lawyers could obtain bail if they can show that, like Enrile, she is not a flight risk because of fragile health and advanced age. Ineluctably, GMA could secure her longed-for temporary liberty through that SC decision, not the much-publicized WGAD opinion. CJ closes with a postscript congratulating his high school chum Filemon T. Berba Jr. for his book 'Leadership for Extraordinary Results': of the 1,200 Mapa High School Class of 1954 graduates, Berba was indisputably the best in math, whose phenomenal grasp of numbers inspired CJ to aspire to be a chemical engineer -- but his strong-willed father compelled him to be a lawyer. CJ has tried to become not just 'a legal technician who tinkers with and repairs legal imperfections' but a 'social engineer who helps build our nation, with law as my basic tool.' Even in his sunset years he still strives to be the engineer that Jun Berba inspired him to be when they were carving their lives in high school. Acclaimed at the book launching, Berba has rightfully become 'the top honcho -- the chief justice, as it were -- of his engineering-management profession. Cheers!'
